claims.text: In single-phase multi-component concentrated alloys, the extent of short-range chemical order governs strength.
Short-range chemical order governs strength by modulating local lattice distortions that impede dislocation motion.
Increasing short-range order reduces the amplitude of local lattice distortions.
Reduced local lattice distortion lowers yield strength relative to a more random as-quenched state.
Increasing short-range order alters deformation behavior relative to a more random as-quenched state.
Rapid quenching produces a nearly random chemical configuration with significant local lattice distortion.
A controlled heat treatment can promote short-range ordering without inducing secondary phases or significant microstructural changes.
Chemical randomness produces larger variations in local lattice parameters than short-range ordering.
Larger variations in local lattice parameters create stronger barriers to dislocation motion.
Stronger barriers to dislocation motion enhance yield strength.
Heat-treated samples with increased short-range order have a more uniform lattice.
A more uniform lattice diminishes barriers to dislocation motion and lowers yield strength.
Short-range ordering may change strain-hardening behavior.
Samples heat-treated to promote short-range ordering should show a statistically significant reduction in yield strength relative to the as-quenched baseline.
Samples heat-treated to promote short-range ordering should show modified strain-hardening rates relative to the as-quenched baseline.
The as-quenched baseline has pronounced local lattice distortions and higher yield strength.
The proposed relationship applies only to single-phase, chemically homogeneous alloys without secondary-phase formation or extensive grain growth.
Diffuse scattering or atom-probe tomography can quantify short-range order.
XRD line broadening or high-resolution TEM can measure local lattice distortion.
Failure to observe a statistically significant yield-strength reduction in confirmed higher-order annealed samples would falsify the proposed mechanism.
